findings.title: [P1] Keep the branch argument out of the shell
findings.body: When `branch` contains shell syntax, such as `main; arbitrary-command`, `exec` interprets it through the system shell and executes the injected command with the application's privileges. The previous `execFile("git", ["show", branch])` invocation passed the value directly to Git without shell interpretation.

findings.title: [P2] Return the Git child directly to preserve cancellation
findings.body: When callers kill the returned process during a long-running `git show`, `exec` may terminate only its wrapper shell while leaving the Git descendant consuming CPU, I/O, and inherited pipes. Returning the direct `execFile` child avoids changing this cancellation behavior.

findings.title: [P2] Kill the Git process rather than only its shell
findings.body:
`exec()` returns the spawned shell process, unlike `execFile()` which returned Git directly. On Linux, calling `.kill()` during a long-running `git show` signals only the shell and can leave the Git descendant consuming CPU/I/O, breaking cancellation semantics.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Pass the branch as an `execFile` argument instead of interpolating it into a shell command
findings.body:
`exec` invokes a shell, so any caller-controlled branch containing shell syntax (for example, `main; rm -rf target`) executes arbitrary commands with the process’s privileges. The previous implementation passed the value directly to Git without shell interpretation.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Keep the branch argument out of the shell
findings.body:
On any deployment passing attacker-controlled branch names, values such as `HEAD; arbitrary-command` are interpreted by `exec` through the system shell, enabling arbitrary command execution with the application’s privileges. The previous `execFile` call passed the branch as a literal argument.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P2] Return the Git child directly so cancellation does not orphan it
findings.body:
`exec()` returns the wrapper shell process rather than `git`. On Linux/macOS, calling `.kill()` on the returned process during a slow or large `git show` can terminate only the shell, leaving Git consuming CPU/I/O and retaining inherited pipes. Repeated cancellations can accumulate orphaned Git processes; `execFile()` previously exposed and killed Git directly.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._
